title: Buffett's 2019 letter: retained earnings, buying good businesses, float, and boards
summary: Buffett explains why GAAP's unrealized-gain rule distorts results and urges focus on operating earnings. He champions retained earnings and compounding, acquisition criteria, insurance float and underwriting discipline, buybacks only below intrinsic value, and critiques board independence and deal-hungry CEOs.

principles.text: Focus on operating earnings and ignore short-term investment gains or losses, realized or unrealized.
principles.quote: Charlie and I urge you to focus on operating earnings – which were little changed in 2019 – and to ignore both quarterly and annual gains or losses from investments, whether these are realized or unrealized.

principles.text: Retained earnings compounding inside good businesses drive long-term value, even when not reported as earnings.
principles.quote: Overall, the retained earnings of our investees are certain to be of major importance in the growth of Berkshire’s value.

principles.text: Buy businesses with good returns on tangible capital, able and honest managers, and a sensible price.
principles.quote: First, they must earn good returns on the net tangible capital required in their operation. Second, they must be run by able and honest managers. Finally, they must be available at a sensible price.

principles.text: Acquisitions are like marriage: buyers are usually the ones surprised, so buy good businesses to begin with.
principles.quote: To achieve a reputation as a good manager, just be sure you buy good businesses.

principles.text: Float is valuable only if underwriting is disciplined; danger always lurks in insurance.
principles.quote: Disciplined risk evaluation is the daily focus of our insurance managers, who know that the rewards of float can be drowned by poor underwriting results.

principles.text: Repurchase stock only when below intrinsic value and ample cash remains; don't prop the price.
principles.quote: Berkshire will buy back its stock only if a) Charlie and I believe that it is selling for less than it is worth and b) the company, upon completing the repurchase, is left with ample cash.
